Chapter 5: Dehumanization and the Erosion of Values.
When you look back, it's natural to wonder—how did it all unravel like this? How did people, who once held strong values, end up crossing lines they’d never imagined?
Most of the time, the answer is found in the slow, almost unnoticed process of dehumanization.
At first, the enemy was just that—someone on the other side. Maybe dangerous, sure, but still a person.
But as days turned into weeks, the language started to shift. Prisoners became “detainees.” Then, they were called “subjects.” Eventually, it was like they weren’t even people anymore.
Under constant stress, with fear and anger piling up, it became easier to see the other side as objects, not individuals.
Picture this: in one unit, soldiers started joking about the people they guarded. On the surface, it was just a way to cope—to make tough days a little lighter.
But those jokes slowly chipped away at empathy. With every laugh, it became easier to justify harsh treatment. Pain started to seem deserved, maybe even necessary.
The rituals of war—the nicknames, the routines, the inside jokes—built up invisible walls, separating “us” from “them.”
What’s striking is, most people didn’t even notice it happening. The change was so gradual, so subtle, that every small step just made the next one a little easier.
The first time someone was mistreated, there might have been hesitation, maybe even a pang of regret. But as it kept happening, it started to feel normal.
The approval of the group began to matter far more than any private doubts.
Now, you might think military training would stop this. After all, soldiers are taught about the laws of war, and the importance of treating prisoners with humanity.
But in the chaos of real conflict, those lessons often get lost. The pressure to fit in, to be part of the team, can be overwhelming.
Some held tight to their values. They refused to take part or spoke up when they saw something wrong. But standing up came with a cost.
They were often sidelined, seen as troublemakers or weak links. And when resistance feels so lonely and risky, most people choose to go along instead.
Here’s something that’s easy to overlook: dehumanization doesn’t just change how soldiers treat the enemy. It changes how they see themselves.
The pride and honor that used to define their service can give way to shame and doubt. The war didn’t just change what they did—it changed who they were.
